description.canonicalEnglish:
Run and manage CPN-based workflow factories.

What:
CPN-based workflow factory CLI for running factories, submitting work, and inspecting live sessions.

How to use:
Run you run --work ./docs/examples/startup-work.json to start the exact Current Factory at ./factory/factory.json with explicit Work and no local server.
Use you server for continuous, non-resumable hosting of the Current Factory API and dashboard. For restart-surviving hosting, use you run --with-server --continuously --record <path>. Add --with-server or --with-site to host one run. See you <cmd> --help for subcommand details.

Agents:
Start with you docs agents for orientation, you submit or you submit batch to enqueue work, and you session list to confirm a live factory.
Run you docs for all packaged reference topics. Use --verbose or --debug for stderr diagnostics; full policy in you docs.

title.canonicalEnglish: Run and manage CPN-based workflow factories

you.flag.debug.usage: emit lower-level command diagnostics where supported (implies --verbose)

you.flag.json.usage: emit structured JSON on stdout for supported commands; diagnostics remain on stderr

you.flag.remote.usage: execute a supported operation through a running You server; does not wait, follow, continue, or start a listener

you.flag.server.usage: factory API base URI (http:// or https://) for HTTP client commands and remote placement; listener-owning commands use --listen host:port for explicit local binds, while local --server binding remains a warned compatibility path

you.flag.verbose.usage: emit concise command diagnostics to stderr

usage.example:
# Start the default Codex-backed Factory with explicit Work.
  you run --work ./docs/examples/startup-work.json

  # Agent orientation and command matrix.
  you docs agents

description.canonicalEnglish:
Route configuration tasks to their canonical commands.

Use `you init` to configure provider/model defaults. Use `you factory config` to validate or transform Factory definitions. Normal runtime initialization materializes packaged/default Factories automatically.

usage.example:
# Configure provider and model defaults.
  you init --provider codex

description.canonicalEnglish:
Inspect live factory runtime state and manage persisted named factories.

Subcommands:
  show     show the current active factory from a running service
  list     list persisted named factories under a factory root
  config   inspect and transform factory configuration
  create   create a named factory from factory.json
  update   replace an existing named factory from factory.json
  replace-current  persist the live current factory from a running service
  delete   remove an unused named factory from disk

Use show against a running service. Use config validate, flatten, and expand for factory configuration inspection and transformation. Use list, create, update, and delete for on-disk named factories under --dir (default factory/). Use replace-current with global --server and --session like show to persist the live current factory.

usage.example:
# Show the active factory from the running service.
  you factory show

  # Validate a factory config before creating or updating it.
  you factory config validate ./factory.json

  # List persisted named factories and which one is current.
  you factory list

  # Create a new named factory from a config file.
  you factory create staging --from ./factory.json --set-current

  # Replace an existing named factory definition.
  you factory update staging --from ./factory.json

  # Delete an unused named factory.
  you factory delete staging

  # Persist the live current factory back to durable storage.
  you factory replace-current

description.canonicalEnglish:
Inspect and transform factory configuration.

Subcommands:
  validate validate a factory.json payload or factory directory
  flatten  write canonical single-file factory config to stdout
  expand   write split factory config layout beside the input file

Use validate before create or update. Use flatten and expand to move between single-file and split-layout factory directories.

usage.example:
# Validate a single-file factory config.
  you factory config validate ./factory.json

  # Flatten a split-layout factory directory.
  you factory config flatten ./factory

  # Expand a canonical factory.json into split layout.
  you factory config expand ./factory.json

description.canonicalEnglish:
Write split factory config layout.

The path may be a standalone factory.json file or a factory directory containing factory.json. The command writes canonical factory.json plus workers and workstations directories beside the input file.

Write canonical single-file factory config.

The path may be a factory directory containing factory.json or a standalone factory.json file. The command writes camelCase canonical JSON to stdout.

Validate a factory.json payload or factory directory through the shared validate-only factory contract used by POST /factory-validations.

Human output lists authored worker and workstation runtime taxonomy values and prints blocking validation targets with inference, agent, script, or poller terminology when worker/workstation pairings are incompatible.

title.canonicalEnglish: Validate a factory config without persisting it

usage.example:
# Validate a single-file factory config.
  you factory config validate ./factory.json

  # Validate a split-layout factory directory.
  you factory config validate ./factory

  # Emit structured validation output for automation.
  you --json factory config validate ./factory.json

description.canonicalEnglish:
Create a new named factory from an existing factory.json file.

The command validates the payload, materializes a new named factory layout under the selected factory root, and refuses to overwrite an existing factory name.

title.canonicalEnglish: Create a named factory from a config file

you.factory.create.flag.dir.usage: factory root directory containing named factories

you.factory.create.flag.from.usage: path to an existing factory.json payload (required)

usage.example:
# Create a new named factory from a config file.
  you factory create staging --from ./factory.json

  # Create and select the new factory as current.
  you factory create staging --from ./factory.json --set-current

  # Emit structured confirmation for scripting.
  you --json factory create staging --from ./factory.json

description.canonicalEnglish:
Delete a persisted named factory from disk.

The command removes the named factory directory under the selected factory root after validation. It refuses to delete the factory currently selected by .current-factory; switch the current pointer to another factory first.

you.factory.delete.flag.dir.usage: factory root directory containing named factories

usage.example:
# Delete an unused named factory.
  you factory delete staging

  # Delete from a custom factory root.
  you factory delete staging --dir my-factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
List persisted named factories stored under a factory root.

By default the command lists project-local named factories from ./factory and writes a human-readable table with each factory name, on-disk directory, and whether it is selected by .current-factory. Global built-ins and customer-edited shared factories live under ~/.you-agent-factory/factories and are listed only when you point --dir there explicitly. The command lists exactly one root at a time and never merges project-local and global entries. Use global --json for scripting output.

you.factory.list.flag.dir.usage: factory root directory containing named factories

usage.example:
# List named factories under the default factory root.
  you factory list

  # List global built-ins and shared factories.
  you factory list --dir ~/.you-agent-factory/factories

  # List factories from a custom root as JSON.
  you --json factory list --dir my-factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
Show the current active factory from a running you-agent-factory service.

By default the command writes a human-readable table with the current factory name and runtime-identifying fields. Use global --json for the API-shaped current-factory payload, and use global --server to target the same factory API base URI as work list and submit. Run you session list to discover live session ids when routing other commands with --session.

you.factory.show.flag.session.usage: target one live factory session; omit to use the default compatibility session

usage.example:
# Show the current factory from the default local service.
  you factory show

  # Emit API-shaped JSON for automation from the default local service.
  you --json factory show

  # Query a factory API on a non-default host or port.
  you --server http://localhost:9090 --json factory show

The command uses global --server and --session like factory show.

  you factory replace-current

description.canonicalEnglish:
Replace an existing named factory from an existing factory.json file.

The command validates the payload, atomically replaces the named factory layout under the selected factory root, and leaves .current-factory unchanged when it already points at the updated name.

description.canonicalEnglish:
Configure the default model provider and optional model used for worker execution, or install a packaged Factory from the embedded catalog.

Supply --provider for non-interactive provider/model setup. Use --package to install a built-in packaged Factory into the named Factory root (default: the global catalog under your home directory).

you.init.flag.provider.usage: registered default model provider (required for non-interactive setup)

you.init.flag.model.usage: optional non-empty free-form default model identifier

you.init.flag.package.usage: public packaged Factory name to install from the embedded catalog

you.init.flag.dir.usage: named Factory root directory for packaged installation

you.init.flag.format.usage: authored root definition format for the installed packaged Factory

you.init.flag.replace.usage: replace an existing packaged Factory directory when the target already exists

usage.example:
# Configure a registered provider non-interactively.
  you init --provider codex

  # Install a packaged Factory into the global named Factory root.
  you init --package @you/goal

description.canonicalEnglish:
Manage factory sessions on a running you-agent-factory service.

Subcommands:
  list       list live sessions, recorded history, or durable Factory Sessions
  show       show one live or durable Factory Session from GET /factory-sessions/{session_id}
  pause      pause one live or durable Factory Session through POST /factory-sessions/{session_id}/pause
  resume     resume one paused live or durable Factory Session through POST /factory-sessions/{session_id}/resume
  create     open another live session from a folder path
  delete     close a live session by session id

Session list output identifies live, durable, and recorded-history provenance. Use --live-only or --history-only to select one source; the two flags are mutually exclusive. Session commands use the same default --port as work list. Use --json to emit API-shaped responses on stdout; diagnostics stay on stderr when --verbose or --debug is set.

title.canonicalEnglish: List, open, and close factory sessions on a running host

usage.example:
# Inspect live sessions through the selected server.
  you session list
  you session show session-beta

  # Lifecycle controls are local by default.
  you session pause
  you session resume
  you session cancel session-beta
  you session terminate session-beta

  # Select an exact already-running server explicitly.
  you --remote --server http://factory.example:7437 session pause session-beta
  you session resume session-beta --remote --server http://factory.example:7437

  # Run output selection and local hosting are separate from placement.
  you --remote --server http://factory.example:7437 run --named @you/research --output primary "Review the current plan"

  # Emit API-shaped JSON for automation.
  you session list --json

  # Open a session on a non-default port and delete through a selected server.
  you session create --dir /workspace/fleet --port 9090
  you --server http://localhost:9090 session delete session-beta --json

  # Target a different service port for list output.
  you session list --port 9090

description.canonicalEnglish:
Open another live factory session from a folder path via POST /factory-sessions.

Use --dir to provide the folder path. Optional --init-new-factory and --validate-only map to the API request fields and are mutually exclusive. Use --target-kind and --target-name when the folder exposes multiple runnable targets. Use --json to emit OpenFactorySessionResponse on stdout; diagnostics stay on stderr when --verbose or --debug is set.

title.canonicalEnglish: Open a live factory session from a folder

you.session.create.flag.dir.usage: folder path to open as a live factory session

you.session.create.flag.init-new-factory.usage: write the default init scaffold at --dir and open a live session

you.session.create.flag.target-kind.usage: target kind when disambiguating runnable factories (default or named)

you.session.create.flag.validate-only.usage: validate the folder and optional target without creating a live session

usage.example:
# Open a session for an existing factory folder.
  you session create --dir /workspace/fleet

  # Validate a folder without opening a live session.
  you session create --dir /workspace/fleet --validate-only

  # Open a named target inside a multi-factory folder.
  you session create --dir /workspace/fleet --target-kind named --target-name beta

description.canonicalEnglish:
Close one live factory session via DELETE /factory-sessions/{session_id}.

Use global --server to select the exact factory API base URI. The legacy --port flag is rejected with guidance to use --server. Use --json to emit a JSON confirmation on stdout.
Manage live Factory Session resource capacity by stable authored Resource.id. Mutable display names and labels are never accepted as resource identity.

examples: you session resource set reviewers 1 session-beta

usage.example: you session resource set reviewers 8

description.canonicalEnglish: Set one live Factory Session resource's capacity by stable Resource.id through POST /factory-sessions/{session_id}/resources/{resource_id}/capacity. The operation is revisioned and idempotent. Use --request-id to replay a known request, --expected-revision to protect against stale state, and --reason for a safe audit reason. Omit session-id for the default compatibility session (~default).

title.canonicalEnglish: Set live Factory Session resource capacity

examples: you session resource set reviewers 8 --request-id raise-reviewers-001 --expected-revision 2
you --json session resource set reviewers 1 session-beta --expected-revision 3

you.session.resource.set.flag.expected-r.usage: effective Factory revision observed before admission

you.session.resource.set.flag.reason.usage: safe operator reason retained with the live change request

you.session.resource.set.flag.request-id.usage: idempotency identity for this capacity request

usage.example:
# Raise the reviewers pool in the default session.
  you session resource set reviewers 8

  # Use an explicit session, revision, and idempotency key.
  you session resource set reviewers 1 session-beta --expected-revision 3 --request-id reviewers-lower-001

description.canonicalEnglish:
List factory sessions and read-only recorded history for the requested scope.

The default scope is all and returns live workspace sessions, durable Factory Sessions, and recorded-history artifacts. Use --live-only for live workspace sessions or --history-only for recorded artifacts. --live-only and --history-only are mutually exclusive. --scope persisted retains the durable Factory Session listing, and --scope history selects recorded history explicitly.

Human output labels each source and JSON output emits ListFactorySessionsResponse on stdout.

title.canonicalEnglish: List live, durable, and recorded factory sessions

you.session.list.flag.live-only.usage: list live Factory Sessions only; mutually exclusive with --history-only

you.session.list.flag.history-only.usage: list recorded Factory Session history only; mutually exclusive with --live-only

you.session.list.flag.scope.usage: session list scope: live, persisted, history, or all

description.canonicalEnglish: Pause one live or durable Factory Session. Local placement is the default; an explicit --server selects one exact already-running You server and implies remote placement, while persistent --remote remains available for explicit remote placement. Omit session-id to target the default compatibility session (~default), pass a named live session id such as session-beta, or pass a durable session id from `you session list --scope all`. Human output reports paused, already-paused, invalid-state, not-found, and unreachable-host outcomes. Placement selects the local or remote adapter; waiting/following and hosting are separate run controls. Use global --json for the API-shaped FactorySessionLifecycleControlResponse.

Human output reports resumed, already-running, invalid-state, not-found, and unreachable-host outcomes. description.canonicalEnglish:
Show one live factory session from GET /factory-sessions/{session_id}.

Human output uses FactorySession as the canonical runtime noun and prints orchestrator kind plus Petri or JavaScript runtime projections. Dynamic workflow wording appears only as JavaScript shorthand. Omit session-id to target the default compatibility session (~default). Use global --json for the API-shaped FactorySession payload and global --server to target the same factory API base URI as work list and factory show.

usage.example:

  # Show one named live session with orchestrator-aware runtime fields.

title.canonicalEnglish: Inspect work from a running factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
Inspect and control work on a running you-agent-factory service.

Subcommands:
  list       list work from GET /factory-sessions/{session_id}/work with optional filters and pagination
  show       show one work item from GET /factory-sessions/{session_id}/work/{work_id}
  move       move one work item to another authored state through POST /factory-sessions/{session_id}/work/{work_id}/move
  render     read a local FACTORY_REQUEST_BATCH JSON file and render its dependency graph to stdout

API-backed list, show, and move commands target the default compatibility session unless --session is set. Use global --json to emit API-shaped responses on stdout; diagnostics stay on stderr when --verbose or --debug is set.

usage.example:
# List work on the default compatibility session.
  you work list

  # Show one work item after submit.
  you work show work-123

  # Render a local batch dependency graph.
  you work render batch.json > graph.mermaid

title.canonicalEnglish: List work from a running factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
List work from a running you-agent-factory service.

By default the command targets the default compatibility session. Use --session to route the request to one specific live factory session instead. Run you session list to discover live session ids.

Optional filters are applied on the server before ordering and pagination. --state matches the current state name exactly (legacy alias: --state-name). --name matches a case-insensitive substring of the work name. --work-type matches workTypeName exactly (legacy alias: --work-type-name). --trace-id matches traceId or currentChainingTraceId exactly. --terminal selects TERMINAL and FAILED work; --non-terminal selects INITIAL and PROCESSING work. The terminality flags are mutually exclusive. Combine all filters with logical AND, plus --max-results and --next-token to page through the filtered result set. --counts adds the total for the complete filtered result set before pagination in human and JSON output. --all includes superseded terminal or failed same-name attempts and identifies each row's successor.

When a Work has a validated workstation result, JSON output exposes it as native structuredResult data, including explicit null. Human output adds a STRUCTURED RESULT column with deterministic compact JSON and leaves it blank when the field is omitted.

usage.example:
you work list

  you work list --name startup --max-results 25

you.work.list.flag.state-name.usage: filter by exact current state name before ordering and pagination

you.work.list.flag.state-type.usage: filter by current state type (INITIAL, PROCESSING, TERMINAL, FAILED)

you.work.list.flag.terminal.usage: select TERMINAL and FAILED work; mutually exclusive with --non-terminal

you.work.list.flag.non-terminal.usage: select INITIAL and PROCESSING work; mutually exclusive with --terminal

you.work.list.flag.name.usage: filter by case-insensitive substring of work name (applied before pagination)

you.work.list.flag.work-type-name.usage: filter by exact workTypeName before ordering and pagination

you.work.list.flag.trace-id.usage: filter by exact traceId or currentChainingTraceId (applied before pagination)

you.work.list.flag.max-results.usage: maximum work items to return per page after server-side filters

you.work.list.flag.next-token.usage: pagination cursor returned by a previous work list response

you.work.list.flag.counts.usage: include total for the complete filtered result set before pagination

you.work.list.flag.all.usage: include superseded terminal or failed same-name work and identify each successor

you.work.list.flag.session.usage: target one live factory session; omit to use the default compatibility session

title.canonicalEnglish: Watch Work state transitions from a running factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
Watch Work state transitions from a running you-agent-factory service.

By default the command targets the default compatibility session (~default). Use --session to route the watch to one specific live factory session instead.

Every stdout line is one complete you.work.watch.v1 NDJSON object with sessionId, eventId, sequence, eventTime, workId, workTypeName, fromState, toState, source, and terminal fields. When a validated structured result first enters canonical Work state, the first following transition line includes optional native structuredResult data, including null; unrelated transitions, failed or unstructured Work, and older recordings omit it. Lines preserve canonical Factory Event order and diagnostics remain on stderr. Finite mode stops after the observed Work cohort reaches terminal states; --follow stays attached until Ctrl-C or parent cancellation. A transient disconnect resumes from the last accepted event ID and sequence with bounded retries, without creating durable watch history or a cursor journal.

usage.example:
# Emit one NDJSON transition per observed Work state change.
  you work watch

  # Keep watching after terminal Work transitions.
  you work watch --session session-beta --follow

you.work.watch.flag.follow.usage: continue watching after observed Work reaches a terminal state

you.work.watch.flag.session.usage: target one live factory session; omit to use the default compatibility session

title.canonicalEnglish: Show one work item from a running factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
Show one work item from a running you-agent-factory service.

By default the command targets the default compatibility session. Use --session to route the request to one specific live factory session instead. Run you session list to discover live session ids.

After submit, use you work list --name <name> to find work ids, then you work show <work-id> to verify one item without JSON pagination.

usage.example:
you work show work-123

  you --json work show work-123

you.work.show.flag.session.usage: target one live factory session; omit to use the default compatibility session

title.canonicalEnglish: Move one work item to another authored state

description.canonicalEnglish:
Move one work item to another authored marking state on a running you-agent-factory service.

By default the command targets the default compatibility session. Use --session to route the request to one specific live factory session instead. Run you session list to discover live session ids.

Moves are rejected while the work item is in an active dispatch. Repeating the same --request-id after a successful move returns 409 without a second mutation.

examples: you work move work-123 ready --request-id op-1

usage.example:
you work move work-123 ready

  you work move work-123 ready --request-id op-1

you.work.move.flag.request-id.usage: optional client idempotency key for operator moves

you.work.move.flag.session.usage: target one live factory session; omit to use the default compatibility session

title.canonicalEnglish: Render a work batch dependency graph as Mermaid

description.canonicalEnglish:
Read a local FACTORY_REQUEST_BATCH JSON file from disk and render its declared work dependencies as a diagram.

The required <batch-file.json> argument is a path to any readable batch file. Graph nodes represent work items; directed edges represent declared dependency relations from the batch.

Output format (default: mermaid):
  mermaid           Raw Mermaid flowchart syntax written to stdout.
  markdown-mermaid  Markdown with a title and one fenced mermaid code block.

This command is read-only. It does not submit work, contact a running factory, or render diagram images.

Redirect stdout to save output, for example:
  you work render batch.json > my-graph.mermaid
  you work render --format markdown-mermaid batch.json > graph.md

usage.example:
# Default: raw Mermaid flowchart to stdout.
  you work render batch.json > my-graph.mermaid

  # Markdown with embedded Mermaid diagram.
  you work render --format markdown-mermaid batch.json > graph.md

description.canonicalEnglish:
Print packaged markdown reference topics from the installed binary.

Run without a topic to print the quick-start blurb and packaged docs index. Use one supported topic argument to print the authored markdown page with no wrapper formatting.

usage.example:
# Print the packaged docs index and quick-start blurb.
  you docs

  # Print one authored reference topic.
  you docs agents

description.canonicalEnglish: Inspect authoritative Worker Session attempts by fleet-wide scope or one Work item. Omit --work-id for the fleet-wide view.

examples: you worker-sessions stream --provider codex --kind session_id --id session-123

usage.example: you worker-sessions list

title.canonicalEnglish: List fleet-wide or Work-scoped Worker Sessions

description.canonicalEnglish: List authoritative Worker Session observations by stable identity. Omit --work-id to inspect the fleet-wide top-level identity surface, or provide --work-id for one Work. Repeat --state values to combine lifecycle states with OR semantics. Use --limit as a positive fleet-wide result bound after filtering. The legacy --max-results and --next-token options are also fleet-wide only. Work-scoped listing does not accept those filters and returns a typed error when they are supplied. The human table shows Work name and ID, Worker Session ID, provider and kind, state, start time, duration, and exit or failure kind. Provider-session identity remains distinct from Worker Session identity. Use --output json for stable machine-readable facts.

usage.example:
you worker-sessions list --output json

  # Work-scoped:
  you worker-sessions list --work-id work-123 --output json

you.worker-sessions.list.flag.work-id.usage: Work identity whose Worker Session attempts should be listed

you.worker-sessions.list.flag.scope.usage: top-level observation scope: omit for fleet-wide, or use direct, factory, or all

you.worker-sessions.list.flag.state.usage: repeatable fleet-wide Worker Session lifecycle state filter. Work-scoped listing does not support this option

you.worker-sessions.list.flag.limit.usage: positive fleet-wide maximum Worker Session observations after scope and state filters

you.worker-sessions.list.flag.max-result.usage: legacy fleet-wide maximum Worker Session observations per page. Prefer --limit

you.worker-sessions.list.flag.next-token.usage: opaque cursor returned by a previous fleet-wide Worker Session list

title.canonicalEnglish: Load workflow and run the factory engine

description.canonicalEnglish:
Load workflow and run the factory engine.

Without an explicit --dir, --named, or --factory selector, you run validates the exact invocation-local ./factory/factory.json as the Current Factory; it does not bootstrap a missing Factory or follow another current-factory pointer. Run you run --work ./docs/examples/startup-work.json to submit explicit default Work; Factory directory runs can consume factory/inputs/task/default while active. Missing and invalid definitions fail before runtime, listener, or browser activation. Ordinary batch, continuous, named, portable Factory, replay, mock-worker, and JavaScript runs start no HTTP listener. Add --with-server to serve the Current Factory API for exactly the run lifetime without opening a browser, or --with-site to imply that server and open the embedded dashboard once after readiness. Server-enabled runs bind only the loopback host and port from --listen host:port when provided; --listen is an exact bind request. Without it, an explicit local --server URI remains a warned compatibility path that can advance monotonically through port 65535 on collisions; report the actual bound URL and join the listener before returning.

Default execution uses batch mode and exits after idle completion. Use --continuously to keep the factory alive while idle until you cancel it. Use --with-mock-workers with an optional JSON config path for deterministic outcomes. Use --worktree <name> to create or reuse a Git worktree under the invocation working directory and execute every worker dispatch in that checkout, independent of provider. Use --quiet to suppress human progress for scripted or CI-oriented runs. Use --skip-permissions to request an invocation-only unsafe permission bypass for agent workers without changing persisted factory configuration. Normal live runs record by default unless you pass --no-record. Replay artifacts are sensitive and can contain prompts, payloads, stdout, stderr, and diagnostic metadata.

Use --named with a persisted canonical factory name to resolve project-local factories before global built-ins under ~/.you-agent-factory/factories. Built-ins materialize lazily into that global root on first use and stay editable on disk. Use --factory with a JSON, YAML, or JavaScript Factory source. Supported selectors are --dir, --named, and --factory. Selected Factories can define custom invocation arguments; run you run --named <factory> --help or you run --factory <factory.yaml> --help to inspect signature-backed usage while keeping existing run-level flags available. In Factory invocation mode, provide either trailing positional text or piped stdin text, or use signature-defined file, repeated, and defaulted inputs; conflicting positional text and stdin return INVOCATION_INPUT_SOURCE_CONFLICT. Named-Factory selection lives in you docs authoring-factories; invocation behavior lives in you docs run and you docs sessions; model choices live in you docs models.

The common ACP workflow is `you run --named @you/goal --provider cursor-acp --model auto "Describe the task"`. Run-level --provider selects modelProvider and --model selects an optional model within that provider. Supported one-shot text invocations use the ordered response stream by default; use --output primary for final-result-only stdout. Human response-stream output lists accepted Work items with IDs/names and available task descriptions, and prints each DEPENDS_ON edge as source depends on -> prerequisite. Active worker progress is stderr-only, with one current line per worker or dispatch and workstation/work IDs when canonical events provide them; eligible TTY output uses spinner frames and deterministic distinct colors, while redirected/non-interactive output is stable and ANSI-free. Use --quiet to suppress progress. Global --json with response-stream selects NDJSON; JSON and NDJSON stdout remain parseable and contain no human-only progress. Quiet conflicts with global JSON and explicit --output. Failures use one standard ErrorResponse on stderr. Runtime logs are structured JSON rolling files grouped by UTC start date under the selected log root; environment details are record-channel diagnostics only, and system logs include command stdout/stderr only on command failures. Runtime metrics are a separate structured JSONL operational channel with independent rolling files.

examples:
# Run a supported operation through an already-running server.
  you --remote --server <uri> run "Review the release notes"

# Start the current Factory with explicit Work.
  you run --work ./docs/examples/startup-work.json

  # Run an existing factory once in explicit batch mode.
  you run --dir factory --work ./docs/examples/startup-work.json

  # Run a persisted named factory from any working directory.
  you run --named @you/tts --output primary "Read the release summary."

  # Run a portable JSON or YAML Factory with a one-shot prompt (see handlingBehavior DEFAULT).
  you run --factory ./factory.yaml "Fix the lint issues"

  # Pipe invocation input via stdin (default primary-result stdout).
  echo "Ship the login bugfix" | you run --named @you/goal

  # Opt into ordered canonical Factory Event progress instead of primary-result-only stdout.
  you run --named @you/goal --output response-stream "Ship the login bugfix"

  # Bind an exact local listener for a server-enabled run.
  you run --with-server --listen 127.0.0.1:7437

title.canonicalEnglish: Upsert a FACTORY_REQUEST_BATCH to a running factory

description.canonicalEnglish:
Upsert canonical FACTORY_REQUEST_BATCH JSON to a running you-agent-factory session.

The document must use type FACTORY_REQUEST_BATCH with at least one works entry. See you docs batch-inputs for the batch schema, relation rules, and examples.

Batch input modes (first match wins):
  --file <path>   read batch JSON from path; use --file - to read stdin
  <path>          read batch JSON from an existing filesystem path (primary form)
  -               read batch JSON from stdin
  <inline-json>   positional whose first non-whitespace byte is { is parsed as JSON
  (no args)       when stdin is not a TTY, read the full piped document from stdin

When both --file and a positional path are provided, --file wins.
When a file path or --file is set, stdin is ignored.

Inline JSON is convenient for small batches; shell argument length limits apply—use a file or pipe for large documents.

Use --dry-run to parse and validate locally, print a summary, and perform no HTTP. Valid --dry-run exits 0 even when the factory is unreachable.

By default the command targets the default compatibility session (~default). Use --session to upsert into one specific live factory session instead.

Global flags (place before the subcommand): --server selects the factory API base URI; --json emits structured success output on stdout; --verbose and --debug emit concise request metadata on stderr without logging batch payload content.

examples:
# Upsert a batch file to the default session.
  you submit batch ./factory/inputs/BATCH/my-batch.json

  # Explicit file flag (wins over a positional path when both are set).
  you submit batch --file ./batches/deploy.json

  # Pipe batch JSON without a temp file.
  cat batch.json | you submit batch

  # Read batch JSON from stdin explicitly.
  you submit batch - < batch.json

  # Validate locally without contacting the server.
  you submit batch --dry-run ./batch.json

  # Target a non-default live session with structured output.
  you --server http://localhost:9090 --json submit batch --session session-beta ./batch.json

usage.example:
# Upsert a batch file to the default session.
  you submit batch ./factory/inputs/BATCH/my-batch.json

  # Explicit file flag (wins over a positional path when both are set).
  you submit batch --file ./batches/deploy.json

  # Pipe batch JSON without a temp file.
  cat batch.json | you submit batch

  # Read batch JSON from stdin explicitly.
  you submit batch - < batch.json

  # Validate locally without contacting the server.
  you submit batch --dry-run ./batch.json

  # Target a non-default live session with structured output.
  you --server http://localhost:9090 --json submit batch --session session-beta ./batch.json

you.submit.batch.flag.dry-run.usage: validate input and print a summary without sending HTTP

you.submit.batch.flag.file.usage: read batch JSON from path; use - to read stdin (wins over a positional path)

you.submit.batch.flag.session.usage: target one live factory session; omit to use the default compatibility session

description.canonicalEnglish:
Host You as an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent over stdio.

ACP clients (editors and IDEs) launch this command as a child process and exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin and stdout. Diagnostics and sanitized startup or serve failures are written to stderr; stdout carries only complete ACP protocol frames.

Cleanly closing stdin (EOF) ends the connection successfully. This command hosts the same production ACP server the process composes through root.BuildProcess; it constructs no second service graph, Chat Sessions service, Factory Sessions service, or transport graph, and it does not start the HTTP or dashboard server.

This is distinct from `you workers acp add|delete`, which configures You's own use of external ACP-speaking provider agents, and from `you server mcp`, which hosts the unrelated Model Context Protocol tool server.

title.canonicalEnglish: Host You as an ACP agent over stdio

usage.example:
# Typical ACP host child-process launch.
  you server acp

description.canonicalEnglish:
Start the dynamic workflow Factory Session MCP server over stdio.

Hosts launch this command as a child process and communicate through newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin and stdout. The default backing service is the deterministic durable session fixture catalog used by workflow CLI commands.

Use --runtime to select the shared durable JavaScript runtime execution service instead of the fixture catalog. Runtime mode requires workflow sources to resolve from the MCP host working directory or an explicit --project-root.

Set the MCP host working directory to the project root where workflow sources and the fixture catalog resolve. See `you docs mcp` for host configuration, serve modes, smoke, and troubleshooting.

title.canonicalEnglish: Start the Factory Session MCP stdio server

you.server.mcp.flag.fixture-catalog.usage: optional path to durable-session contract fixtures; defaults to the catalog discovered from the current working directory

you.server.mcp.flag.project-root.usage: project root for workflow source resolution in --runtime mode; defaults to the current working directory

you.server.mcp.flag.runtime.usage: select the shared durable JavaScript runtime execution service instead of the fixture catalog

usage.example:
# Typical MCP host child-process launch.
  you server mcp

  # Explicit fixture catalog for offline smoke outside the repository root.
  you server mcp --fixture-catalog ./pkg/transports/http/testdata/durable-session-contract-fixtures.json

  # Runtime-backed serve against live durable JavaScript execution.
  you server mcp --runtime
